subject: Science and Technology (Environmental Science)

chunks.content: Living things share seven key life processes, often remembered by the acronym MRS GREN: Movement, Respiration, Sensitivity (responding to surroundings), Growth, Reproduction, Excretion (getting rid of waste), and Nutrition (taking in food/energy). A thing is classified as living if it can do all of these over its lifetime. Non-living things (rocks, water, a chair, a car) may show one or two of these features (a car 'moves' and 'excretes' exhaust) but not all seven, and they do not grow, reproduce, or respond to stimuli on their own the way living organisms do.
learning_activities: Sorting picture cards of objects into living and non-living groups
Testing objects in the local environment against the MRS GREN criteria
Discussing borderline cases such as seeds or dormant organisms

chunks.content: Living things are broadly classified into the plant kingdom and animal kingdom. Animals are further grouped into vertebrates (with a backbone: mammals, birds, reptiles, amphibians, fish) and invertebrates (without a backbone: insects, spiders, worms, molluscs). Plants are grouped into flowering plants and non-flowering plants (such as ferns and mosses). Classification is based on shared observable characteristics: mammals have fur/hair and feed young on milk; birds have feathers and lay hard-shelled eggs; reptiles have dry scaly skin; amphibians live both in water and on land and have moist skin; fish live in water and breathe through gills.
learning_activities: Sorting local animals into vertebrate groups by their features
Building a simple classification key for plants and animals found around the school
Comparing an insect (6 legs, 3 body parts) with a spider (8 legs, 2 body parts)

chunks.topic: Parts of a Flowering Plant and Their Functions
chunks.content: A typical flowering plant has roots (anchor the plant and absorb water and minerals from the soil), a stem (supports the plant and transports water/nutrients between roots and leaves), leaves (make food through photosynthesis, using sunlight, water and carbon dioxide to produce glucose and oxygen), and flowers (the reproductive part, containing male parts - stamens producing pollen - and female parts - the pistil/carpel, which develops into fruit containing seeds after fertilisation).
learning_activities: Dissecting a flower to identify and label its parts
Growing bean seeds and observing root, stem and leaf development
Diagramming water's path from roots to leaves

chunks.content: Photosynthesis is the process by which green plants make their own food. Using chlorophyll (the green pigment in leaves) to capture energy from sunlight, plants combine carbon dioxide (taken in from the air through tiny pores called stomata) with water (absorbed by the roots) to produce glucose (a sugar used for energy and growth) and oxygen (released back into the air as a by-product). The word equation is: carbon dioxide + water --(sunlight, chlorophyll)--> glucose + oxygen. This process is essential for nearly all life on Earth, since it is the primary source of atmospheric oxygen and the base of most food chains.
learning_activities: Testing a leaf for starch (a product of photosynthesis) using iodine solution
Demonstrating that a plant kept in the dark makes less starch than one in sunlight
Drawing and labelling the photosynthesis word equation

chunks.content: Living things go through a life cycle - a series of stages from birth/germination to death, often including reproduction. A butterfly's life cycle has four stages: egg, larva (caterpillar), pupa (chrysalis), and adult butterfly - a process called complete metamorphosis. A frog's life cycle (also metamorphosis) goes egg, tadpole (with gills, living in water), tadpole growing legs, and adult frog (with lungs, living on land and water). A flowering plant's life cycle goes seed, germination, seedling, mature plant, flowering, pollination and fertilisation, and seed production, which restarts the cycle.
learning_activities: Sequencing picture cards of the butterfly or frog life cycle
Growing and recording the germination and growth stages of a bean plant
Comparing complete metamorphosis (butterfly) with incomplete metamorphosis (grasshopper, which has no pupa stage)

chunks.content: The human body is organised into systems that work together. The skeletal system (bones) supports the body and protects internal organs (e.g. the skull protects the brain, the ribcage protects the heart and lungs). The muscular system works with bones to produce movement. The digestive system (mouth, oesophagus, stomach, small and large intestines) breaks down food into nutrients the body can absorb and use. The circulatory system (heart, blood vessels, blood) pumps blood around the body to deliver oxygen and nutrients and remove waste. The respiratory system (nose, trachea, lungs) takes in oxygen and removes carbon dioxide through breathing. The nervous system (brain, spinal cord, nerves) controls and coordinates the body's actions and senses.
learning_activities: Labelling a diagram of the human skeleton and naming major bones
Measuring pulse rate before and after exercise to observe the circulatory system at work
Tracing the path of food through the digestive system on a diagram

chunks.content: A food chain shows how energy passes from one living thing to another, starting with a producer (a green plant, which makes its own food via photosynthesis), then to a primary consumer (herbivore, which eats plants), then a secondary consumer (carnivore/omnivore, which eats the herbivore), and sometimes a tertiary consumer (top predator). Arrows in a food chain point in the direction energy flows (e.g. grass -> grasshopper -> frog -> snake -> eagle). A food web shows how multiple food chains in an ecosystem interconnect, since most animals eat and are eaten by more than one other species. Decomposers (bacteria, fungi) break down dead organisms and waste, returning nutrients to the soil.
learning_activities: Constructing a food chain from a set of local plants and animals
Building a food web by connecting several overlapping food chains
Discussing what happens to a food chain/web if one species is removed

chunks.content: A balanced diet includes carbohydrates (energy, e.g. sadza, rice, bread), proteins (growth and repair, e.g. meat, beans, fish, eggs), fats (energy storage and insulation), vitamins and minerals (regulating body processes, e.g. from fruits and vegetables), and water. Good personal hygiene practices - regular hand washing (especially before eating and after using the toilet), bathing, brushing teeth, and keeping nails short and clean - prevent the spread of disease-causing germs (bacteria, viruses, fungi, parasites). Common ways diseases spread include contaminated water and food, unwashed hands, insect bites (e.g. malaria from mosquitoes), and contact with an infected person.
learning_activities: Sorting foods into a balanced-diet food group chart
Demonstrating correct handwashing technique and explaining why it matters
Discussing how common local diseases (e.g. malaria, diarrhoea) spread and can be prevented

chunks.content: Matter exists in three common states: solid (has a fixed shape and volume; particles are tightly packed and vibrate in place, e.g. wood, rock, ice), liquid (has a fixed volume but takes the shape of its container; particles are close together but can move past each other, e.g. water, oil), and gas (has no fixed shape or volume, spreading to fill its container; particles are far apart and move freely, e.g. air, steam). Matter can change state: melting (solid to liquid, by heating), freezing (liquid to solid, by cooling), evaporation (liquid to gas, by heating), condensation (gas to liquid, by cooling), and sublimation (solid directly to gas, e.g. dry ice).
learning_activities: Observing and recording ice melting into water and water boiling into steam
Sorting classroom objects by state of matter
Drawing a diagram of the water cycle showing the state changes involved

chunks.content: Materials are chosen for particular uses based on their properties: strength (resists breaking, e.g. steel for construction), hardness (resists scratching, e.g. diamond, stone), flexibility (bends without breaking, e.g. rubber, some plastics), transparency (lets light through, e.g. glass), conductivity (allows heat or electricity to pass through, e.g. metals conduct well; wood, plastic and rubber are insulators that resist the flow of heat/electricity), absorbency (soaks up liquid, e.g. cloth, paper), and waterproofing (resists water, e.g. plastic, some fabrics treated with wax). Materials can be natural (wood, cotton, wool, clay) or man-made/synthetic (plastic, nylon, glass).
learning_activities: Testing a set of materials for strength, flexibility and water absorbency
Sorting materials into natural and man-made groups
Matching materials to appropriate uses based on their properties (e.g. why umbrellas are waterproof)

chunks.content: A mixture is formed when two or more substances are combined without a chemical reaction, so each substance keeps its own properties and can usually be separated again. Common separation techniques include: filtration (separating an insoluble solid from a liquid using a filter, e.g. sand from water), evaporation (separating a dissolved solid from a liquid by heating off the liquid, e.g. salt from salty water), sieving (separating solids of different particle sizes, e.g. stones from sand), magnetism (separating magnetic materials like iron filings from a mixture), and decanting (carefully pouring off a liquid from a settled solid). A solution is a special mixture where one substance (the solute) fully dissolves in another (the solvent), such as sugar dissolved in water.
learning_activities: Separating a mixture of sand and water by filtration
Separating salt from salty water by evaporation
Using a magnet to separate iron filings from a sand-iron mixture

chunks.content: Energy exists in many forms: kinetic energy (movement energy, e.g. a moving car), potential energy (stored energy due to position or condition, e.g. water behind a dam, a stretched rubber band), heat/thermal energy, light energy, sound energy, electrical energy, and chemical energy (stored in food and fuels). Energy can be transformed from one form to another but, according to the law of conservation of energy, it cannot be created or destroyed - only changed in form. For example, a torch converts chemical energy (from the battery) into electrical energy, then into light and some heat energy.
learning_activities: Identifying energy transformations in everyday devices (torch, radio, car)
Demonstrating potential energy becoming kinetic energy with a ball rolling down a ramp
Discussing renewable (solar, wind, hydro) versus non-renewable (coal, oil, gas) energy sources

chunks.content: Simple machines make work easier by changing the size or direction of a force. The six classical simple machines are: the lever (a rigid bar that pivots on a fulcrum, e.g. a see-saw, crowbar, scissors), the wheel and axle (e.g. a doorknob, a bicycle wheel), the pulley (a wheel with a rope/chain, used to lift loads, e.g. a well bucket system, a flagpole), the inclined plane (a sloped surface that makes it easier to move a load up or down, e.g. a ramp), the wedge (two inclined planes joined back to back, used to split or cut, e.g. an axe, a knife), and the screw (an inclined plane wrapped around a cylinder, e.g. a bolt, a jar lid).
learning_activities: Identifying examples of each simple machine in the classroom or home
Building a simple lever and testing how the fulcrum's position affects the force needed
Comparing the effort needed to lift a load directly versus using a ramp

chunks.content: A force is a push or pull that can change an object's speed, direction, or shape. Key types include: gravity (pulls objects towards the Earth's centre, giving them weight), friction (resists motion between two surfaces in contact, e.g. why a ball rolling on grass slows faster than on a smooth floor), magnetism (attraction or repulsion between magnetic materials, e.g. iron, nickel; like poles repel, unlike poles attract), and air resistance/water resistance (a form of friction that slows objects moving through air or water, e.g. why a parachute falls slowly). Forces are measured in newtons (N).
learning_activities: Testing how different surfaces (grass, tile, sand) affect friction using a toy car
Investigating magnetic attraction and repulsion between bar magnets
Discussing why gravity keeps objects on the ground and pulls falling objects downward

chunks.content: Electricity flows through a complete, unbroken loop called a circuit. A simple circuit needs a power source (e.g. a battery), a conductor (wire, usually made of a metal like copper, which allows electric current to flow), and a component such as a bulb or buzzer. A switch can open (break) or close (complete) the circuit to turn the component off or on. In a series circuit, components are connected in a single loop, so if one bulb fails the whole circuit breaks; in a parallel circuit, components are connected on separate branches, so each operates independently of the others. Insulators (rubber, plastic, wood) do not allow current to flow and are used to make electrical equipment safe to handle.
learning_activities: Building a simple circuit with a battery, wire and bulb to light it up
Comparing series and parallel circuits by building both and observing bulb behaviour
Testing which everyday materials are conductors and which are insulators

chunks.content: Weather is the day-to-day state of the atmosphere in a place (e.g. today it is hot and rainy), while climate is the average weather pattern of a region over many years (e.g. Zimbabwe has a subtropical climate with a distinct rainy season, roughly November to March, and a dry season for the rest of the year). Weather elements measured include temperature (using a thermometer), rainfall (using a rain gauge), wind speed and direction (using an anemometer and wind vane), and cloud cover. Zimbabwe's seasons are typically described as the warm/rainy season (roughly November-March), the cool/dry season (April-August), and the hot/dry season before the rains (September-October).
learning_activities: Recording daily weather observations (temperature, rainfall, cloud cover) over a week or month
Making a simple rain gauge and measuring rainfall
Comparing Zimbabwe's seasons and their typical weather patterns

chunks.content: The water cycle describes how water continuously moves between the Earth's surface and the atmosphere. Key stages: evaporation (the sun heats water in oceans, rivers and lakes, turning it into water vapour that rises into the air), transpiration (water vapour released from plant leaves, often grouped with evaporation as 'evapotranspiration'), condensation (water vapour cools high in the atmosphere and turns back into tiny water droplets, forming clouds), precipitation (water falls back to Earth as rain, hail, sleet or snow), and collection/runoff (water flows into rivers, lakes and oceans, or soaks into the ground as groundwater, ready to evaporate again and repeat the cycle).
learning_activities: Drawing and labelling a water cycle diagram with all stages
Setting up a simple evaporation-condensation demonstration with a covered cup of water in the sun
Discussing how the water cycle connects to rainfall patterns and water conservation

chunks.content: Soil forms over long periods through the weathering (physical and chemical breakdown) of rocks, combined with decomposed organic matter (humus) from dead plants and animals. Main soil types by particle size are: sandy soil (large particles, drains water quickly, holds few nutrients), clay soil (very fine particles, holds water well but drains poorly and can become waterlogged), and loamy soil (a balanced mixture of sand, silt and clay, generally considered the most fertile for farming as it retains both moisture and nutrients while still draining adequately). Soil layers (horizons) typically include topsoil (richest in organic matter, best for plant growth), subsoil, and bedrock at the base.
learning_activities: Testing local soil samples for texture (sandy, clay, loamy) by feel and a simple settling test in water
Comparing how quickly water drains through different soil types
Discussing why loamy soil is generally preferred for crop farming

chunks.content: The solar system consists of the Sun (a star, at the centre, providing light and heat through nuclear fusion) and the objects that orbit it: eight planets (in order from the Sun: Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, Neptune), their moons, dwarf planets (such as Pluto), asteroids, and comets. Earth is the third planet from the Sun and the only known planet to support life, due to its distance from the Sun (allowing liquid water), its atmosphere, and its magnetic field. Earth rotates on its axis once approximately every 24 hours, causing day and night, and orbits the Sun once approximately every 365.25 days, causing the year and (combined with Earth's tilted axis) the seasons.
learning_activities: Ordering the eight planets from the Sun and comparing their relative sizes
Modelling day and night using a torch (Sun) and a rotating globe (Earth)
Discussing why Earth's tilt causes the seasons to change through the year

chunks.content: Natural resources are materials or substances occurring in nature that people use, classified as renewable (can replenish naturally within a human lifetime, e.g. water, forests, sunlight, wind, soil if managed well) or non-renewable (form over millions of years and are used up faster than they form, e.g. coal, oil, natural gas, minerals). Conservation practices to protect natural resources include afforestation/reforestation (planting trees), avoiding overgrazing and deforestation, water conservation (avoiding waste, protecting water sources from pollution), recycling and reducing waste, and sustainable farming practices (crop rotation, contour ploughing to prevent soil erosion). Environmental issues connected to poor resource management include soil erosion, deforestation, water pollution, and loss of biodiversity.
learning_activities: Sorting local natural resources into renewable and non-renewable categories
Investigating causes and effects of soil erosion in the local area and possible solutions
Planning a simple school conservation project such as a tree-planting or recycling initiative

chunks.content: Technology is the application of scientific knowledge to solve practical problems and meet human needs, ranging from simple tools (a hoe, a wheelbarrow) to complex systems (computers, the internet, mobile phones). The technology/design process typically follows: identifying a problem or need, researching and generating possible solutions, designing and planning (including sketches or models), making/building the solution, testing it, and evaluating and improving it based on results. Information and Communication Technology (ICT) - computers, tablets, mobile phones, the internet - is increasingly integrated into science learning for research, data recording, simulations and communication.
learning_activities: Working through the design process to solve a simple local problem (e.g. designing a water carrier)
Building and testing a simple model (e.g. a bridge from straws, a simple water filter)
Using ICT tools to research a science topic or record experimental data

chunks.content: Under the Heritage-Based Curriculum, learners study various digital devices and ICT tools used in daily life. This includes personal computers (desktops and laptops), mobile devices (smartphones and tablets), and peripheral devices like printers, scanners, and digital cameras. Key skills involve identifying these tools, understanding their functions (input, process, output, storage), and using them responsibly. Digital devices help in searching for information, creating documents, and communicating with others. Awareness of basic software, file management, and internet safety (cyber-wellness) is essential for modern learners.
learning_activities: Identifying and naming parts of a computer system
Practising basic typing and mouse skills
Discussing the uses of smartphones and tablets in the community
Learning to stay safe online and protecting personal information

chunks.content: Safety signs use standard shapes and colours to convey their meaning at a glance: red circles with a diagonal line indicate prohibition (something not allowed); yellow triangles indicate warning/caution (a hazard to be aware of); blue circles indicate mandatory action (something that must be done, e.g. wear protective equipment); green squares/rectangles indicate safe conditions or emergency information (e.g. exit routes, first aid). In science activities, basic safety practices include not tasting or smelling unknown substances, handling sharp or hot objects with care, washing hands after experiments, and telling a teacher immediately about spills or breakages.
learning_activities: Matching safety sign shapes and colours to their meanings
Identifying safety signs found around the school and community
Discussing safe practices to follow during a simple science experiment
